Lessons.Title: Describing and Graphing Situations
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: distinguish functional from nonfunctional relations using unique outputs per input, identify independent/dependent variables and use descriptive graphs to model a changing situation. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 4 Lesson 1, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/4/1/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). The source uses bagel purchase choices and a dog on a leash; this lesson preserves reasoning about possible outputs and graph shape with independently authored datasets rather than publisher artwork.

Original first-party bicycle-charge scenario: a rental bicycle costs $4 unlock fee plus $3 per elapsed hour, with whole hours h≥0, so price P(h)=4+3h dollars. The pairs (0,4),(1,7),(2,10),(3,13) are functional: for each h exactly one total. Asking only 'total price of rental' with unspecified duration yields many totals, but that does not invalidate the function because the input must be stated.

Contrast a nonfunction relation R={(1,5),(2,7),(2,9),(3,11)}. Input 2 is paired with two different outputs 7 and9; no unique output can be determined. A graph with two points vertically aligned at x=2 fails the vertical-line test. Distinguish multiple inputs giving one output, which is allowed: Q={(0,4),(1,4),(2,7)} is functional despite output 4 appearing twice.

Original motion story: during seconds 0–2 a remote toy moves away from a post at 2 metres per second; seconds 2–5 it stays 4 metres away; seconds 5–7 it approaches at 2 metres per second. Its distance graph is piecewise increasing, constant, decreasing. For any fixed elapsed time 0≤t≤7 it has exactly one distance; it does not matter whether the same distance occurs at different times.

Student task: sketch the toy motion graph and independently label rates, classify three different tables as functions or nonfunctions, construct a counterexample relation and explain why it fails. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for input/output definition, valid classification with evidence, correctly labelled motion graph and reasoned verbal critique (8 maximum). Do not claim a publisher photograph or actual physical motion was reproduced.

V12 source-equivalent first-party bundle-price discussion: a bakery sells individual rolls for $1.60, a six-pack for $7.20 and a twelve-pack for $12.80. For exactly 13 rolls, different purchase plans yield different totals: 13 singles cost $20.80; two six-packs and one single cost $16.00; a twelve-pack plus one single costs $14.40; one six-pack plus seven singles costs $18.40. Each plan is feasible. Students defend one interpretation and critique why input "number of rolls" alone does NOT select a unique total without a purchase-policy input; under cheapest-price policy there is exactly one price for each integer quantity.

V12 function and graph task: label an actual input-output table for bike hours h=0,1,2,3 and cost P(h)=4+3h, then draw its points. In a second plotted relation, include (2,7) and (2,9) at the same input to show why the vertical line at x=2 intersects twice. Explain the difference between one output per fully specified input and a single y-value repeated for different inputs. Interpret x and y coordinates and state relevant whole-hour domain.

Publisher student lesson uses alternative bagel purchase plans and graph narratives including motion of a leashed animal; independently invented examples preserve the key ambiguity/function-property comparison without source pixels. Draft teacher rubric0–2 each for graph and axes, uniqueness argument, contextual model comparison and independent written explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Function definition
KeyConcepts.Definition: A relation is a function when every permitted input maps to exactly one output.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A repeated output is allowed; two different outputs for one input are not.
KeyConcepts.Example: P(h)=4+3h gives one price for each whole-hour h.

KeyConcepts.Title: Input and output
KeyConcepts.Definition: The independent input determines a dependent output under the model.
KeyConcepts.Example: Hours h is input; dollar charge P(h) is output.

KeyConcepts.Title: Graph uniqueness
KeyConcepts.Definition: A vertical line crossing a relation at two distinct y-values signals nonfunction.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check whether a single x has multiple y-values.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check a rental table
WorkedExamples.Question: Is P(h)=4+3h a function and what are outputs for h0,1,2,3?
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.
Steps: Each input has one value by the equation.
Therefore table relation is a function.
WorkedExamples.Check: Every input occurs with one output.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find nonfunction evidence
WorkedExamples.Question: Is R={(1,5),(2,7),(2,9),(3,11)} a function?
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.
Steps: Since 7≠9, there is not a unique output for input2.
A vertical line x=2 would meet two points.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No, R is not a function.
WorkedExamples.Check: Two distinct outputs share the same input.

WorkedExamples.Title: Represent toy movement
WorkedExamples.Question: Find toy distance at t=1,3,6 seconds in a piecewise motion.
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.
Steps: From0 to2 sec, d(t)=2t, so d(1)=2 metres.
From2 to5, d=4, so d(3)=4 metres.
From5 to7, d=4−2(t−5), so d(6)=2 metres.
Points are connected by up, horizontal, down segments.
Each time still has one distance.
WorkedExamples.Check: All distances in allowed time interval are 0–4 metres.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming two inputs may not share one output
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Only one input having multiple outputs violates the definition.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling an entire physical scenario nonfunctional because time changes
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Time is explicitly an input and output changes with time.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Fix one time and ask whether the output is unique.

SummaryPoints: A function assigns exactly one output to every input in its domain.
Tables and graphs may display multiple repeated outputs without violating uniqueness.
Motion can be increasing, constant and decreasing and remain a function.
Teacher reviews graphs and explanations, not just arithmetic.
